name: Rolling Forecasts
title: Rolling Forecasts
answer: Rolling forecasts are a financial planning practice that replaces a fixed annual budget with a continuously updated outlook, usually covering the next twelve to eighteen months. Each month or quarter, the forecast horizon extends by one period so the organisation always looks the same distance ahead. The scope includes revenue, operating costs, cash flow, and key business drivers rather than every general ledger line. It is used by finance teams to support decisions about hiring, capital spending, and pricing.

sections.body: Rolling forecasts are a financial planning practice that replaces a fixed annual budget with a continuously updated outlook, usually covering the next twelve to eighteen months. Each month or quarter, the forecast horizon extends by one period so the organisation always looks the same distance ahead. The scope includes revenue, operating costs, cash flow, and key business drivers rather than every general ledger line. It is used by finance teams to support decisions about hiring, capital spending, and pricing.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on existing financial planning systems, spreadsheets, or cloud planning platforms that can hold driver-based models and version history. Data is drawn from the general ledger, CRM, payroll, and operational systems, often through scheduled extracts or APIs. The infrastructure must support frequent refresh cycles, scenario storage, and access controls so different departments see only their relevant parts. Because the forecast is updated often, the platform needs to handle overlapping versions without overwriting the prior approved view.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with a baseline forecast built from actual results and then applies assumptions about volumes, prices, headcount, and other drivers. Each period, the finance team replaces the oldest month or quarter with a new one, updates actuals, and re-runs the model. Driver-based modelling is common, meaning revenue is calculated from units and price rather than entered as a single number. Variance analysis compares the new forecast to the previous one and to the annual plan, so changes are explained rather than hidden.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are version confusion, unclear ownership of assumptions, and over-reliance on a single model that no one has validated. Finance teams usually keep an audit trail of who changed each assumption and when, and they separate the approved forecast from working drafts. Provenance matters because a rolling forecast feeds board packs, loan covenants, and investor updates, so the source data and the logic behind each driver should be documented. Access rights should limit who can change assumptions, while still allowing business partners to see the output.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Rolling forecasts are moving away from static annual cycles toward continuous planning, with more frequent updates and shorter close-to-forecast times. Machine learning is beginning to help by suggesting driver values or flagging unusual variances, but the core discipline remains human judgement about the business. The likely direction is tighter links between operational plans and financial forecasts, so a change in sales pipeline or production schedule updates the outlook automatically. Finance teams will spend less time assembling data and more time testing scenarios and advising the business.
